extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural designers, and students concerned with ornament and moulding in building design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for designing, placing, and managing architectural ornament (mouldings, chamfers, fillets, dogtooth, etc.), with attention to scale, material, regional style, and the unity/discipline of decoration. Emphasises treatment of angles, edges, rolls/recesses, and distribution of ornament across a building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of limitation / willing submission
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of this type does not consist in the mere shutting of the ornament into a certain space, but in the acknowledgment by the ornament of the fitness of the limitation — of its own perfect willingness to submit to it; nay, of a predisposition in itself to fall into the ordained form, without any direct expression of the command to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merely force natural forms into geometric cages. The form must internally 'accept' the prescribed law (Ruskin's hawthorn-and-triangle analogy). Ornament should appear to grow into and with the limiting form; transgressions are permissible only as instances of deliberate, exceptional permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience to internal headship / unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Obedience to internal headship, which constitutes the unity of ornament; alternation of shade with light forms one of the chief elements of continuous ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design ornament to have an internal organizing principle (unity). Use alternation of light and shade (e.g., dentils, billet mouldings) to produce continuous, pleasing ornament that supports the whole composition, even if its symbolic meaning is not consciously apprehended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must have purpose — avoid gaps and redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: There must never be any sense of gap or blank, neither airy sense of there being a single member, or fragment of a member, which could be spared. Whatever has nothing to do, whatever could go without being missed, is not ornament; it is deformity and encumbrance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute ornament so no part of the building looks accidentally unfinished or redundantly decorated. Either diffuse ornament in due relation across the whole, or concentrate it deliberately on chosen features. Avoid patchy alternation between luxuriance and sudden blankness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity vs. manageability
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot have too much if it be good; but you may easily have too much if you have more than you have sense to manage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every additional order of ornament raises the difficulty of discipline. Only increase ornamentation within the limits of what the designer and builders can coherently govern — otherwise it will hinder the whole composition (Ruskin's army analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure your capacity to govern ornament (discipline/control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of ornament consists in its being governed. Lose your authority over it, let it command you, or lead you, or dictate to you in any wise, and it is an offence, an incumbrance, and a dishonor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be modest in ambition: add orders of ornament only as long as there is no chance of 'mutiny.' The architect must control ornament; it must not run away from the designer's intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place ornament in the fittest parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some parts of the building, without ornament, are more painful than others, and some wear ornament more gracefully than others; there are general laws respecting the parts of a building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose locations for ornament based on where it will most gracefully and effectively relieve or enhance the architecture. Understand which elements can bear decoration and which cannot; unexpected ornament can be pleasurable but is best used knowingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify building parts for decoration (five divisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Class together (a) the base of the wall and of the shaft; (b) the wall veil and shaft itself; (c) the cornice and capital; (d) the jamb and archivolt (including arches and aperture jambs); (e) the roof (real roof and minor roofs of pinnacles and gables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five functional/positional divisions as the organizing frame when planning ornament for the whole building, since different treatments suit different parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special treatment for corners (the Angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The corner is an awkward feature; how to turn a corner gracefully becomes a perfectly general question, to be examined without reference to any particular part of the edifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corners require particular consideration and dedicated moulding strategies (e.g., chamfers, beads, rolls). Don't ignore corner-treatment—they can determine the character of the whole elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six fundamental moulding forms for furrows and ridges
rubrics_metrics.description: Furrows and ridges used to obtain parallel light and shade must present one or more of six forms: square projection, square recess, sharp projection, sharp recess, curved projection, curved recess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize which of the six basic moulding types you are using. On small scale these may constitute the whole ornament; on large scale they often need additional sub-ornament to avoid insipidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify moulding subjects to three general types
rubrics_metrics.description: For separate consideration there are only three subjects: 1. The Angle. 2. The Edge and Fillet. 3. The Roll and Recess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing mouldings, reduce complexity by thinking in terms of these three categories and design their ornament accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chamfer treatments for corners: concave, straight, convex
rubrics_metrics.description: A corner may be cut off (chamfered) in three ways: with a concave cut, with a straight cut, or with a convex cut. The first two produce two milder corners; the convex chamfer substitutes a soft curve and gets rid of the corner altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the chamfer type according to desired visual effect. Concave/straight chamfers are summary and create paired corners; convex (gentle) chamfers remove the corner but risk appearing weathered unless intentionally marked. Consider scale, finish, and the building's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate intentional bluntness with an incised line
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that the bluntness is our own ordaining, we will put a slight incised line to mark off the rounding, and show that it goes no farther than we choose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using convex/rounded chamfers that might suggest wear, add a deliberate incised line or similar mark to demonstrate that the form is intentional and crafted, not accidental erosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic and regional appropriateness of chamfers and mouldings
rubrics_metrics.description: Shallow chamfers are peculiar to southern work (Venice/Verona) and may be derived from incised angles; deep chamfers are characteristic of northern work and may imitate angle shafts; French examples go deeper still.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose moulding and chamfer types that suit the regional/ stylistic tradition of the building and the character you want: shallow, delicate profiles for southern/Italian work; deeper, more robust chamfers for northern/Gothic traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edge and fillet decoration should suit function and material
rubrics_metrics.description: A fillet (like a boat gunwale) serves a protective or projecting function and will not admit of rich ornament in rough service; its simplest ornament may be a series of notches alternating on each edge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let function determine ornament complexity: heavily-used or exposed edges require simpler, more durable decoration; delicate fillets in protected positions may be more elaborate. Use fillet ornament to express the object's use and material honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dogtooth and edge ornament — orientation, scale, and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The plain dogtooth (pyramids formed by meeting notches) is used in profusion; its effect varies with orientation (front-facing, oblique, one side horizontal) and scale. It is often a foil for other ornament rather than a complete decorative solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose dogtooth depth, pitch, and orientation to achieve desired light/shadow and distance effect (e.g., zigzag at distance). Use dogtooth to set off finer ornament above or to give vigor to less detailed elements; avoid overusing it where it would dominate unduly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrich dogtooth and adapt to northern/Italian types
rubrics_metrics.description: By deepening the Italian cutting one gets the Northern type; oblique or curved cuts yield extravagant decorative possibilities (leaves, tracery, demons, owls, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dogtooth can be elaborated into many motifs. Increase carving depth and add subsidiary arcs/triangular cavities to turn simple pyramids into leaf-forms or more intricate Northern tracery, but respect scale and viewer proximity to avoid incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fillet enrichment within Venetian incrustation traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Venetian architecture is of incrustation: thin marble pieces project under the arch face forming a narrow band or fillet which invites enrichment. The dogtooth had not been invented by Byzantine architects and would not be used here if it had been, because the dogtooth alone can give a building a peculiar look.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working with incrusted materials (marble over brick), choose enrichments for fillets that suit the incrusted character and do not impose an incongruous overall expression. Consider the projection of soffit pieces and how the fillet band will read in light and from typical viewpoints; avoid ornament (e.g., dogtooth alone) that would dominate or mischaracterize the whole building.
